segments.text: Outside the walls of Troy stands a giant wooden horse. The Greeks, it seems, have sailed away and left it behind as a gift. But inside, soldiers are waiting for the night. It is one of the most famous stories ever told, and many people remember it from Homer's Iliad. Yet the Iliad ends before the horse is ever built. So where does the story of the Trojan horse come from?

segments.text: The Iliad is one of the oldest works of Greek literature. It tells of only a short time in the tenth year of the Trojan War, beginning with the anger of the hero Achilles. It ends not with the fall of Troy, but with a funeral. In one old translation, its final line reads: "Thus held they funeral for Hector tamer of horses."

segments.text: The horse does appear in Homer's other great poem, the Odyssey. Far from home, Odysseus sits at a feast and asks the blind singer Demodocus to sing of the wooden horse, which Epeius built with the help of the goddess Athena. In the song, the Trojans argue over what to do with it: break it open, throw it down onto the rocks, or keep it as an offering to the gods.

segments.text: Other early Greek poems told the end of the war, such as the Little Iliad and the Sack of Troy. They do not survive in full. We know them mainly through short summaries written centuries later. Yet those summaries already have the horse taken into the city through a broken wall, the Trojan priest Laocoön killed by serpents, and Sinon, a Greek who helps to deceive the Trojans.

segments.text: The version most of us know comes from Rome. About two thousand years ago, the poet Virgil wrote the Aeneid. In its second book, the Trojan hero Aeneas tells a queen of his city's last night. The priest Laocoön warns, in one old translation, "I fear the Grecians even when they offer gifts," and hurls his spear at the horse. Sinon tells a convincing lie. Serpents come from the sea. And the Trojans open their own walls to pull the horse inside.

segments.text: Virgil wrote many centuries after Homer's poems, and he told the story from the side of the defeated. He did not invent the horse, the serpents, or Sinon. But many of the scenes we picture today, the warning, the lie, the opened wall, come to us most vividly through his telling.

segments.text: At least one ancient writer offered another explanation. In the second century AD, the travel writer Pausanias saw a bronze statue in Athens, called the Wooden Horse. He wrote that anyone who did not think the Trojans utterly foolish knew the horse had really been a machine for breaking through the wall. And how many men were inside? One later handbook gives fifty, but adds that the author of the Little Iliad said three thousand.
